newsitem.title: CANADA: MacMillan Bloedel sees improvement in 1997.
newsitem.headline: MacMillan Bloedel sees improvement in 1997.

text.p: MacMillan Bloedel Ltd said on Tuesday that it expected strong markets for certain products in the first half of 1997 after Canada's biggest lumber and paper company reported heavy fourth-quarter losses.

"Looking ahead to 1997, we see strong markets for our high value specialty lumber products through the first half of the year and good demand for building materials in North America," MacMillan chief executive Bob Findlay said in a statement. MacMillan reported a loss of C$0.60 a share in the quarter, compared to a year earlier C$0.50 a share profit.
The fourth-quarter results also included C$66 million in restructuring costs and asset writedowns.

Of that amount, C$45 million was related to the writedowns of old boilers being replaced at the Powell River, British Columbia paper mill in 1997 and MacMillan's investment in a cement fiber operation in Oregon (American Cemwood).
The remaining C$21 million was for costs related to streamlining the corporate head office and the business units.
The fourth-quarter loss was within the range of analysts' forecasts for a loss of between C$0.42 and C$0.69 a share.
MacMillan said net earnings for the year fell to C$0.36 a share from C$2.08 a share in 1995.
"The combined effect of the decline in prices for pulp logs and chips, panelboards and packaging products reduced operating earnings by approximately C$280 million," Findlay said.

Earnings from the solid wood business were down C$199 million to C$81 million in 1996, due to a combination of higher harvesting costs, lower revenues from pulp logs and chips and a weaker yen. MacMillan estimated C$140 million was added to 1996 logging costs due to regulatory changes.
MacMillan was currently in discussions with the British Columbia government to relieve the impact of regulations on logging costs, Findlay said.

The packaging business contributed only C$19 million in operating earnings in 1996, down from C$172 million in 1995. Packaging prices dropped sharply in 1996 with the average price of linerboard down 30 percent during the year.
Findlay said he expected a gradual improvement in packaging in 1997.
The company's paper operations contributed C$44 million in operating earnings in 1996, up from C$39 million in 1995.
But high inventory levels in North America and reduced consumption caused paper prices to deteriorate in 1996, MacMillan said.

Findlay said the outlook for paper was slowly improving as industry inventories returned to normal levels. A newsprint price increase of US$75 a tonne has also been announced for late in the first quarter of 1997.
"Although we expect to see some improvement in our markets during 1997, we need to further reduce costs to generate an acceptable return on assets," Findlay said.
